title: Handel's Messiah
hookLine: an oratorio sewn together from the King James Bible, first performed for charity in Dublin

cards: A hall in Dublin, packed. The organizers have asked the ladies not to wear the wide hooped skirts of the day, and the gentlemen to leave their swords at home, so more people can squeeze in.

The money from the tickets is going to charity. On the stage, singers and an orchestra, and a new piece by a German composer living in London, George Frideric Handel. No costume, no acting, no plot in the usual sense.
Just singers and players and, word after word, the Bible.

teach.b: Messiah is an oratorio: sacred words set to music for concert singers, without staging. Handel didn't write the words.
A friend of his, Charles Jennens, assembled them, choosing rather than composing, from the King James Bible and the Prayer Book psalms. Isaiah's comfort ye. The shepherds in the fields.
Behold the Lamb of God. I know that my redeemer liveth. It tells the whole story of Christ, from promise to birth to death to rising, using only scripture.
At the close of the second section comes the Hallelujah chorus. Its words come from the book of Revelation.

teach.h: ALLELUIA: THE LORD GOD OMNIPOTENT REIGNETH.
teach.b: In the King James Bible, chapter nineteen: "Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth."

teach.h: HE SHALL REIGN FOR EVER AND EVER.
teach.b: Then, from chapter eleven, the line that gives today its carry: "The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever."
Handel sets that last phrase so it comes round again and again, the voices overlapping, as if nobody can quite stop saying it. A custom goes with it.
In some places, audiences stand for the Hallelujah chorus. Tradition says a king once stood at that moment, and everyone stood with him. There's no firm record that it happened.
People stand anyway. What they're standing for is a line from the last book of the Bible: the kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord.

how: Choirs and churches perform Messiah each year, especially around Christmas and Easter, and some cities hold sing-along performances where the audience joins the choruses.

games.q: you're organizing the first performance of a new oratorio in a packed Dublin hall. how do you fit more people in?
o: ask the ladies to skip hooped skirts and the gentlemen to leave their swords.
sell standing room in the aisles.
games.why: the organizers asked for no hooped skirts and no swords, so more people could squeeze in, and the money went to charity.

practice: Play a recording of the Hallelujah chorus if you can, or read the two lines from Revelation slowly, and listen for the moment when he shall reign for ever and ever starts to repeat and overlap.
If you pray, let it be your praise, and stand if you'd like to; if not, simply listen to an old, sung claim about whose kingdom lasts.

wordCard.voice: Handel's Messiah. An oratorio by George Frideric Handel, with words drawn entirely from scripture, first performed for charity in Dublin, and remembered for its Hallelujah chorus.

orig.note: Hebrew: praise ye the LORD — hallel, praise, and Yah, a short form of God's name.
